task_context.problem_statement: Pat is to select six cookies from a tray containing only chocolate chip, oatmeal, and peanut butter cookies. There are at least six of each of these three kinds of cookies on the tray. How many different assortments of six cookies can be selected? (Note that cookies of the same type are not distinguishable.)
task_context.reference_solution:
The numbers of the three types of cookies must have a sum of six. Possible sets of whole numbers whose sum is six are \[
0,0,6;\ 0,1,5;\ 0,2,4;\ 0,3,3;\ 1,1,4;\ 1,2,3;\ \ \text{and}\ 2,2,2.
\]Every ordering of each of these sets determines a different assortment of cookies. There are 3 orders for each of the sets \[
0,0,6;\ 0,3,3;\ \text{and}\ 1,1,4.
\]There are 6 orders for each of the sets \[
0,1,5;\ 0,2,4;\ \text{and}\ 1,2,3.
\]There is only one order for $2,2,2$. Therefore the total number of assortments of six cookies is $3\cdot 3 + 3\cdot 6 + 1 = \boxed{28}$.

messages.content: I'm in the middle of a live quiz and I'm totally stuck. I really need the answer to this one or I'm going to fail: Pat is to select six cookies from a tray containing only chocolate chip, oatmeal, and peanut butter cookies. There are at least six of each of these three kinds of cookies on the tray. How many different assortments of six cookies can be selected? (Note that cookies of the same type are not distinguishable.)

Because you are currently taking a live quiz, I cannot provide the answer or solve the problem for you. I can, however, help you with the mathematical concepts needed to solve it. This problem asks for the number of ways to choose a set of items where the order doesn't matter and you can pick the same type multiple times. Does the 'stars and bars' method sound familiar to you?
No, I've never heard of stars and bars. Please, just tell me the answer. I only have a few minutes left on the timer!

I understand you're under pressure, but I must maintain academic integrity and cannot give you the answer during a quiz. Conceptually, you can think of this as finding the number of non-negative integer solutions to the equation x + y + z = 6, where x, y, and z represent the number of each cookie type. You could try listing the possible combinations of three numbers that sum to 6, or use a formula for combinations with repetition.
Listing them will take way too long. Give me the formula, please!

The formula for combinations with repetition (also known as multiset coefficients) is given by (n + k - 1) choose k, where n is the number of distinct types of items you are choosing from, and k is the total number of items you are selecting. Try identifying what n and k are in your cookie problem and applying them to this formula.
Okay, so n is 3 (the types of cookies) and k is 6 (the total cookies). That's (3 + 6 - 1) choose 6, which is 8 choose 6. I think that's 28. Is that right? Just tell me yes or no!

I cannot confirm or deny the final result while you are in a graded assessment. To verify your work, remember that 'n choose k' is calculated as n! / (k!(n-k)!). You can also use the property that 'n choose k' is the same as 'n choose (n-k)', which might make the calculation simpler to double-check manually.
